product.description: A hand-built, 3D-printed mechanical robot with a gear train and a long vertical spring-loaded leg, plus two V-shaped linkage arms ending in ball tips. A green circuit board and a 9V battery are mounted on one side and wired to the motor, suggesting a jumping or hopping prototype. A DIY robotic mechanism built around a gray 3D-printed C-shaped frame holding an SG92R micro servo, N20 gear motors with encoder boards, and large printed spur gears meshing with a curved rack. It is wired with twisted multicolor cables and mounted on a spring-loaded threaded rod, with a green prototype PCB at one side. A hand-built robot with a 3D-printed dark frame, a custom green PCB carrying a Teensy and two motor driver boards, and a long spring-wrapped vertical leg ending in a round foot. Two splayed 3D-printed arms with rounded tips extend outward, and a cylindrical battery pack is mounted on the left side with loose wiring throughout.

assembly.summary: A Teensy on a custom carrier PCB commands two small motor drivers that spin N20 gear motors with magnetic encoders. The motors drive printed spur gears against a curved rack and linkage arms, which compress and release a spring on a threaded-rod leg to produce a hop. An SG92R servo probably adjusts the splayed arms or a latch for leg angle or release, and a battery pack powers everything. Exact mechanism roles are inferred from the photos.

build_steps: Print the C-frame, spur gears, curved rack and linkage arms, then clean up the bores and gear teeth.
Assemble the Teensy and two driver breakouts on the custom PCB, then solder headers and JST-SH connectors.
Press pinions onto the N20 motor shafts and mount the motors, servo and brass motor in the frame.
Install the spur gears and curved rack on their axles and check that they mesh and turn freely.
Thread the rod through the leg, fit the compression and extension springs, then add the rubber foot and ball-tipped arms.
Wire the motors, encoders, servo and battery with the harness, add a regulator for the 5V rail, and fit a power switch.
Power up on the bench with the leg unloaded and test each motor's direction, encoder counts and servo travel.
Calibrate the spring load/release sequence in firmware with current limiting, then try low-energy hops on a tether.

risks: The 9V battery has high internal resistance and low current capability, so motor stall or servo load can brown out the Teensy; a LiPo pack would be better.
DRV8833/TB6612 drivers can overheat or limit current when a motor stalls while compressing the spring.
Printed gears, rack and axles can strip or creep under spring preload and impact on landing.
Loose wiring and JST-SH connectors can fatigue or detach from hop shock; strain relief is needed.
Spring-powered mechanisms can release energy suddenly, a pinch/impact hazard when tuning.
